extracted.intended_audience: Undergraduate students in discrete mathematics / transition-to-proof and algorithm design courses
extracted.subtask_description: A course project combining historical reading (Euler, Lamé) with modern graph-theoretic reformulation: (a) analyze and prove results about Euler paths/circuits and (b) derive, implement and analyze methods for counting polygon triangulations (Catalan numbers). Tasks include reading, paraphrase, proof-writing, worked examples, Java/programming tasks, empirical timing and algorithmic analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restate Euler's 'occurrences' definition in modern degree terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewrite Euler’s definition of 'the number of occurrences of the letter denoting that area' in terms of the degree of a vertex deg(v). (Euler's original: if deg(v) is even, then v occurs 1/2 deg(v) times; if deg(v) is odd then v occurs half the number increased by one.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show the equivalence between Euler’s counting-of-letters procedure and counting incident edges (degree). Explain the parity cases (even/odd) and how they map to Euler’s written procedure. Compare notation and terminology with contemporary 'degree of a vertex'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply Euler's stepwise procedure to decide Euler-path existence
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow Euler’s algorithm: label areas A,B,C,..., write total bridges + 1, list number of bridges leading to each area, mark areas with even degree, for evens write half the number, for odds write half the number+1, sum these values and compare to total bridges+1 to decide if an Euler journey is possible and where it must start.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Execute the six-step procedure exactly on a given map/graph; identify starting area when sum is one less than bridges+1 (must start from an asterisk/area with even degree) or when equal (start from an unmarked/odd-degree area). Apply to provided examples (Königsberg, 15-bridge example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reformulate Euler's observations in degree-theoretic language
rubrics_metrics.description: Translate Euler's paragraph-based observations (e.g., 'numbers next to letters add to twice total number of bridges') into modern graph-theory statements about sum of degrees and parity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State and explain the Handshake Theorem: sum of degrees = 2|E|. Derive corollaries such as 'a graph has an even number of odd-degree vertices' and connect them to Euler's narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: State and apply simplified existence rules for Euler paths/circuits
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the simplified rules: (i) if more than two vertices have odd degree then an Euler trail is impossible; (ii) if exactly two vertices have odd degree then an Euler trail exists starting at one of the odd-degree vertices; (iii) if no vertices have odd degree then an Euler circuit exists starting at any vertex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate application to examples and explain why the parity counts determine existence. Provide counterexamples and edge cases (e.g., disconnected graphs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Critically evaluate Euler's original proofs and claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess how convincing Euler's original definitions and arguments are (e.g., his claim that 'the total of all the occurrences equals number of bridges plus one'), and compare his proof style to a modern textbook proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss rigor, implicit assumptions (such as connectedness), use of parity arguments, where Euler's reasoning is heuristic, and how a modern proof would fill gaps or reframe steps. Point to specific paragraphs (9–13, 16–19) and explain differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate the necessity of connectedness in modern theorem statement
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain and illustrate why the modern theorem requires G to be connected (e.g., show a disconnected graph with all even degrees that nonetheless has no Euler circuit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give an explicit counterexample (two disjoint even-degree components) and argue formally why no single Euler circuit can traverse edges in separate components. Relate to Euler's original text and identify where connectedness is implicitly used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a modern proof of the 'if' direction (Hierholzer proof sketch completion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Complete the provided proof sketch: if G is connected and all degrees are even, then G contains an Euler circuit. Address the case-splitting, construction of initial circuit, removal of its edges, handling connected components, and eventual combination into a circuit visiting every edge exactly once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the Case I/II structure: handle loops-only case, choose a vertex incident with a non-loop, construct a simple circuit, remove its edges, apply induction or component-wise circuit insertion, and prove termination and edge coverage. Use the appended lemmas as needed and answer the italicised guiding questions in the sketch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write a careful modern proof of the 'only if' direction and corollary
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume G has an Euler circuit; prove every vertex has even degree (only if). Then prove the corollary for Euler paths: a connected graph has an Euler trail iff it has ≤2 odd-degree vertices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove counting/enter-exit pairing of edges at each visit to a vertex; formalize why degrees must be even for circuits and why a trail can have exactly two odd-degree endpoints. Provide clear structure and justification for each step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Lemma I and Lemma II correctly in proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply Lemma I (repeated edge implies repeated vertex in a walk) and Lemma II (existence of simple path between any two vertices in connected graph) as tools in constructing proofs and arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite and use the lemmas where the proof requires converting arbitrary walks to simple paths or arguing about repeated edges/vertices. Explain how corollary of Lemma I gives absence of repeated edges in vertex-simple walks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct an Euler path/circuit when existence is known (constructive algorithm)
rubrics_metrics.description: When conditions guaranteeing existence hold, produce an explicit traversal (sequence of vertices/edges) that is an Euler path or circuit, e.g., using the deletion-and-splicing idea Euler sketches (or Hierholzer's algorithm).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate the construction on examples (including the 15-bridge example), document the steps, and justify correctness. Discuss Euler's suggestion of mentally removing paired bridges and show how it maps to modern procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain and prove the Handshake Theorem in comparison to Euler's discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: Locate and present the Handshake Theorem: sum of degrees = 2|E|. Compare textbook proof with Euler’s argument in paragraph 16 and comment on differences in rigor and presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a one- or two-paragraph modern proof, then contrast with Euler's counting-of-letters approach, noting succinctness and implicit assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define triangulation and count properties (triangles and diagonals)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an n-sided convex polygon, define a triangulation and prove by induction that any triangulation uses n-3 diagonals and divides polygon into n-2 triangles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear definitions (diagonals connect non-adjacent vertices, noncrossing), give base case and inductive step, and present examples (e.g., ABCDEF) to illustrate counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive Lamé's recurrence (formula (1)) by 'base-side' decomposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain Lamé's first counting approach: fix an arbitrary side as a base, consider the vertex opposite making the triangle with that base, and sum counts of decompositions of the two resulting polygons to derive the recurrence for P_{n+1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewrite and justify equation (1) in your own words, show how grouping by which vertex forms the triangle with the fixed side partitions decompositions, and produce the explicit convolution-style recurrence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive Lamé's alternative counting (formula (2)) by 'special vertex' enumeration
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow Lamé's second counting method: for a chosen vertex, enumerate decompositions by diagonals incident to it, analyze double-counting, and derive formula (2) relating the total sum over vertices to P_n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully account for multiplicities: show how many times a given triangulation is counted across all vertex-based enumerations (use the fact each triangulation has n-3 diagonals with 2(n-3) ends), and derive the division factor that yields formula (2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine the two counting formulas to obtain closed-form Catalan expression (formula (3))
rubrics_metrics.description: Use formulas (1) and (2) to deduce the simpler recurrence or closed form for P_n (Catalan number identity) and show the algebraic steps leading to formula (3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carry out the algebraic manipulation in detail (as in the text) and explain why the final formula is more efficient for computation. Then derive the binomial closed form (Catalan number expression) and demonstrate equivalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute small Catalan values by hand and enumerate triangulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the recurrence to compute P_i for i = 2,...,8 and draw/list all triangulations for n = 4,5 (and classify those for n=6 according to recurrence groups).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show a table of computed values and provide explicit drawings/diagonals for small n. For n=6, partition triangulations into groups corresponding to terms in the recurrence and label which group each triangulation belongs to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove growth inequalities for P_n (e.g., P_{n+1} ≥ 2 P_n and P_n ≥ 2^{n/8})
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide simple mathematical proofs of stated growth lower bounds for the Catalan sequence (observational claim P_{n+1} ≥ 2 P_n for n≥3 and formal proof that P_n ≥ 2^{n/8}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use recurrence relations and simple inequalities to derive the stated bounds. Explain each inequality step clearly and indicate any induction or combinatorial reasoning used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implement naive recursive computation of P_n (SRCAT) and report empirical timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Write a simple recursive function that computes P_n directly from the recurrence (1) (no memoization), then run repeated invocations to record the time to compute P_i for increasing i (stop when 10-minute limit reached) and tabulate i vs time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe programming language used (Java recommended but optional), testing methodology, time measurement approach, and present a table of results; report largest i (N0) computed within time limit and observed time growth pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implement recurrence (3) direct recursive computation (ASRCAT) and time it
rubrics_metrics.description: Write a recursive routine implementing formula (3) directly, measure running times for P_i similarly (10-minute cap), and report largest i (L0) computable and timings table.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeat the empirical methodology of SRCAT, compare runtimes with SRCAT, and discuss numerical stability/efficiency differences introduced by using formula (3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Implement memoized / dynamic programming computation and measure improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Implement a dynamic programming (store-and-reuse) algorithm to compute P_i iteratively or with memoization, time repeated computations under the same 10-minute constraint, and report largest i (M0 or L1) attainable and timing table.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain storage strategy, present timing table and graphs, compare growth rates to naive recursive and formula-based recursive implementations, and justify why DP yields better scalability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce and analyze graphs of timings and discuss algorithmic complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: Graph timing tables obtained for naive recursion, recurrence (3) recursion, and dynamic programming implementations; analyze and compare growth rates and practical effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include plotted curves (or printouts), interpret asymptotic behaviour (exponential vs polynomial), discuss crossover points, and connect observed runtimes to combinatorial growth (Catalan numbers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discuss implications of combinatorial growth for algorithmic feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain how the number of triangulations (Catalan growth) impacts the feasibility of the naive generate-and-test algorithm for optimal triangulation and how dynamic programming addresses the computational challenge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relate lower bounds (e.g., exponential growth) to time complexity of naive enumeration, contrast with DP's polynomial-time approach for weighted optimal triangulation (explain which problems remain intractable), and provide practical recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document programming experiments and reproducibility
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting program timings and maximal computable indices, include implementation details, time measurement technique, machine specs/limits, and code description so results are reproducible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State language and version, hardware & OS, compilation flags, timing library used, input ranges, and any optimizations or truncations applied. Present tables with i and timings in seconds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain results and derivations in your own words
rubrics_metrics.description: For reading and derivation tasks, paraphrase Lamé/Euler arguments, explain reasoning steps in plain language, and relate historical approaches to modern ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address specific prompts like 'explain in your own words' and 'comment on how a modern textbook proof might differ'; avoid mere copying—show understanding by rephrasing and exemplifying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answer instructor-oriented reflective questions and compare sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow instructor prompts: compare Euler's proofs with modern texts, locate the Handshake Theorem in textbooks, comment on pedagogical uses and suitability for course levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite modern textbooks where theorems are presented, summarize differences in proof style, and discuss where in a course (beginning discrete math, transition to proof, algorithms) the project fits best. Suggest classroom modalities (group vs individual).
